title: Dihedral Group
body:
$D_n$: the symmetries of a regular $n$-gon, meaning every rigid motion that leaves the shape
occupying the same space. There are $2n$ of them.

$$D_n = \{e, r, r^2, \dots, r^{n-1},\; s, rs, r^2s, \dots, r^{n-1}s\}$$

$n$ **rotations** by multiples of $2\pi/n$, and $n$ **reflections**. The count is easy to see
without listing: a symmetry can send vertex 1 to any of $n$ places, and then the shape is either
flipped or not, so $n \times 2$.

## The presentation

Two generators and three relations describe the whole group:

$$r^n = e, \qquad s^2 = e, \qquad srs = r^{-1}$$

The third one is the group being non-abelian, written down. **Reflect, rotate, reflect back and
the rotation has reversed**, which is exactly what happens if you flip a piece of paper over,
turn it, and flip it back. Equivalently $sr = r^{-1}s$, and that rule is all you need to
multiply any two elements: push every $s$ to the right, flipping the exponent of $r$ each time
it passes one.

```
D_4, the square
    rotations   e, r, r², r³        (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°)
    reflections s, rs, r²s, r³s     (2 through opposite vertices,
                                     2 through opposite edge midpoints)
    order 8, non-abelian
    r·s ≠ s·r : one is a flip about one axis, the other about another
```

## Structure

- **The rotations form a [[Cyclic Group]]** $\langle r \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}_n$, a
  [[Subgroup]] of index 2. The reflections are the other [[Coset]] and are not a subgroup, since
  two reflections compose to a rotation.
- **Every reflection has order 2** and is its own inverse. The order of $r^k$ is $n/\gcd(n,k)$.
- $D_n \le S_n$: a symmetry permutes the $n$ vertices, so $D_n$ sits inside the
  [[Symmetric Group]]. For $n \ge 4$ it sits strictly inside, since $2n < n!$; not every
  rearrangement of the vertices is a rigid motion, because most break adjacency.
- $D_3 = S_3$, order 6 either way. The triangle is small enough that every vertex permutation is
  a symmetry, and it is the smallest non-abelian group.

## Why it is the example the course keeps using

$D_n$ is the smallest family where the group axioms describe something you can hold. Symmetry of
a physical object *is* a group: composing two symmetries gives a symmetry (closure), undoing one
is a symmetry (inverses), and doing nothing is one (identity). Every abstract statement about
non-commutativity, cosets, and subgroups can be checked here by turning a square over in your
hands, and that is why it appears in every worked example alongside $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
